text: Say the bottles come back and the recycler can't find a buyer. What does the deposit buy us then?
author: Codex writer B

text: It still gives people a reason to pick up the empties. I'd want to know who's buying the plastic, too.
author: Codex writer B

text: Getting a bottle off the roadside is worth doing. Selling the material is a separate job.
author: Codex writer B

text: We could fill a warehouse with bottles nobody wants. I'd want a buyer lined up before asking stores to take them.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's my concern. A refund gets the bottle across the counter. I'd want to know who takes it from there.
author: Codex writer B

text: Where would you put the empties if you ran a grocery with no spare room?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask whether stores could share a return site. I want the deposit, and a cramped shop deserves an answer.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd bring a grocer in before we settle the collection arrangements. We can start with the floor space a return takes.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd have to give up room I use for something else. That's a cost I'd count before voting yes.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd walk the stockroom with the owner. Until I knew what had to move, I couldn't ask for that space.
author: Codex writer B

text: What should I tell a school club that raises money by turning in bottles if we vote to end the deposit?
author: Codex writer B

text: Tell them to check the scrap price before they set a fundraising goal. They couldn't count on the refund anymore.
author: Codex writer B

text: They'd lose the deposit income. I favor ending it, but I wouldn't tell those students their cans will bring the same money.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd tell them that's one reason I'm voting to keep it. They know what a bag of empties will bring.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask the club to show us its receipts. Before we take that refund away, I'd like the room to see what it pays for.
author: Codex writer B

text: If we end the deposit, would you give stores extra time to collect on refunds they've already paid?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want a settlement date in the text. A store that's already paid its customers deserves time to file.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd give the stores a chance to settle up. The last day to bring a bottle back needn't be the last day to submit a claim.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's a loose end I want settled before I'd vote to repeal. Paying out at the till and getting reimbursed take different amounts of time.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the deposit until we can tell a shopkeeper how to collect what's owed.
author: Codex writer B

text: How is a cashier supposed to tell which bottle earns a refund when the bottles look alike?
author: Codex writer B

text: Print the refund on the bottle. A clerk ought to be able to turn it over and show the customer.
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with what the shopper can see. If the label is all that tells the drinks apart, put the refund there too.
author: Codex writer B

text: Try explaining that at the till with a line behind you. I wouldn't give the cashier that job until we settle what counts.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd send the coverage list back to committee. People ought to know when they buy a drink whether they'll get their money back.
author: Codex writer B

text: A distributor marks the bottles and a grocer takes them back. Which job would you pay for?
author: Codex writer B

text: Pay the grocer for taking them back. Marking a case for sale is work the distributor can price into the shipment.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let both bring in their costs. Marking a whole case takes different work from counting loose bottles at the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: Show me the grocer's bill for taking returns before we promise anybody an allowance.
author: Codex writer B

text: I could support paying the clerk who does the sorting. Paying the distributor on top of that would need a case of its own.
author: Codex writer B

text: What happens to the deposit on a bottle I buy the night before repeal takes effect?
author: Codex writer B

text: You paid it. Give people time to bring those bottles back, and post the last return day where the drinks are sold.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the counter open for old bottles after stores quit charging the deposit on new ones.
author: Codex writer B

text: You ought to get that money back when you've finished the drink. That's one reason I'll vote to keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd vote against a cutoff that lets a store charge me on Friday and turn me away on Saturday.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose a household has no recycling pickup. Where do you expect them to take the empties after repeal?
author: Codex writer B

text: A county drop-off could take them. Before we print directions, somebody needs to check which sites actually take glass.
author: Codex writer B

text: That depends on where they live. I'd ask each county to name a place that takes bottles and tell us which towns would be left out.
author: Codex writer B

text: Right now they can take them back on a grocery trip. Show me where the next trip would end before we vote that away.
author: Codex writer B

text: If nobody can name a place nearby that takes glass, I'd leave that family the store counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: I support it. Let the distributors pick up each other's empties so a grocer can clear the stockroom in one trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm with the member. I'd like to hear from the corner shops about where a shared return counter could go.
author: Codex writer B

text: Put the refund on the label and let people claim what they paid. I'll vote for that.
author: Codex writer B

text: I can't support it until we know who pays when the empty goes back to a different distributor.
author: Codex writer B

text: Stand behind a customer with a sack of cans and one clerk at the till. That's why I'm voting no.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd give the bottlers until the next session to bring us a litter plan before I put a deposit on drinks.
author: Codex writer B

text: I share that doubt. I'd need to see a buyer for the plastic before I'd support collecting it this way.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm on the same side. I'd like a bottler to show us the return trip on a map before we vote to fill those trucks.
author: Codex writer B

text: Counting and sorting take paid time. Until the grocer can tell me who covers those wages, my vote is no.
author: Codex writer B

text: I favor a refund you can collect wherever that kind of drink is sold. Who keeps track of the store where they bought a soda?
author: Codex writer B

text: If the coverage is confusing, fix the label. That's a poor reason to give up on the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd give the deposit a chance. Could the distributors share a pickup so the store doesn't have to wait on each truck?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd end it too. A grocer could use that room for groceries again.
author: Codex writer B

text: I favor repeal. I'm reserving judgment on when a shop should have to file its last claim.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, end the deposit. Just give people a fair chance to bring back bottles they've paid on.
author: Codex writer B

text: Until you can tell a family where else to take glass on their grocery trip, I'm voting to keep the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep it. A club collecting cans can count on the refund when it plans a field trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: Why throw the refund out? I'd hear a proposal to pay stores for handling bottles.
author: Codex writer B

text: I agree. Somebody who paid the deposit ought to decide when to bring the bottle back.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm wary of taking the store out of the picture. A county site can be a long drive.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund too. A bag of cans is worth carrying home when you know what you'll get for it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd let the shopkeeper have the stockroom back. I'll vote to end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: We can stop charging on new bottles and still honor the old ones. I support repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd end the refund and ask which county sites could take the glass. I'd want those addresses posted before the last return day.
author: Codex writer B

text: That would help the grocers. I'd have the distributors work out who credits the shop when the bottles go back on somebody else's truck.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd invite a shop owner to walk us through that trip. A shared counter has to be somewhere customers can get to.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. A parent buying juice ought to be able to tell right there in the aisle what the empty bottle is worth.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a settlement between the distributors answer that? A customer can't tell which truck brought the bottle.
author: Codex writer B

text: Then let's hear what size return a small shop can take at once. That clerk shouldn't have to turn away everybody with empties.
author: Codex writer B

text: What would you do next session if all we get from the bottlers is another request for time?
author: Codex writer B

text: That's the testimony I'd want too. An order for the plastic tells us more than a picture of a full bin.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. I'd put the trip back to the filling plant on that same map. An empty takes up room on a truck too.
author: Codex writer B

text: Exactly. A store can't make payroll with the deposit it hands back to a customer.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who would settle up with a shop that pays out on a brand it never stocked? That's the part I want in writing.
author: Codex writer B

text: Which drinks would earn that mark? The label comes after somebody has made that choice.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would that truck take everybody's bottles on the same day? A grocer needs to know when the space will be clear.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. That's room the store could use even if it never sold another bottle.
author: Codex writer B

text: Fair enough. I'd hear from the people who check the claims before setting the deadline.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd put the last return date on the store door while people can still bring their bottles in.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the county had a glass bin at the grocery, would that answer your objection, or is it the refund you want to keep?
author: Codex writer B

text: What would the club get for its cans at the scrap dealer? I'd like to see the difference before we decide what those trips stand to lose.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who would pay the handling allowance? I don't want to tell a shopkeeper we've settled that while the check still has no name on it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. Someone who buys drinks by the case may still have full bottles on the shelf when the cutoff comes.
author: Codex writer B

text: How far is the round trip for somebody at the edge of the county? That's what I'd put beside the address.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's why I'd keep it. A kid picking up cans shouldn't need to follow the scrap market to know whether the trip is worth it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a regular pickup clear enough room for that shopkeeper? I'd try that before ending every customer's refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: How would the clerk tell an old bottle from one sold after the change if the packages still look alike?
author: Codex writer B

text: An address tells you where the bin is. How does someone who walks to the store get their bottles out to the county site?
author: Codex writer B

text: Give an empty can a refund and a school club can collect it for the trip fund. The club can work out what a bag is worth before anybody goes knocking. That's why I'm voting for {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: {presiding}, a grocer has every right to ask who'll take the bottles away. Distributors can share that pickup. I want us to make the return trip work, and I'll vote for the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: When you pay a deposit, you ought to be able to walk back into a store with your empties and get it back. That's the promise I'd vote to make with {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: If we put a deposit on a drink, somebody buying it ought to know at the shelf whether they can claim a refund. I support {bill-name}, and I want that clear before the first bottle comes back.
author: Codex writer B

text: {presiding}, imagine running a corner grocery. Where would you put a day's worth of returns while you wait for a truck? That space has to come from somewhere. I'll vote against {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Somebody has to stand at the counter and count the bottles. Somebody else has to haul them away. Until I know how both get paid, I can't ask this chamber to adopt the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: I can see how a bottle gets from the store to the recycler. What happens if the recycler has a warehouse full and no buyer for the plastic? I can't support {bill-name} with that question open.
author: Codex writer B

text: Picture a cashier holding bottles that look alike. How does the customer know why only one earns a refund? I'd like an answer that works at the counter before I vote for a deposit. Today my vote is no.
author: Codex writer B

text: Consider a grocer who stores returns in the stockroom. I'd give the owner that space back. That's a reason to vote for repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: I favor ending the deposit. Before we're done, I want the grocer who pays the last customer a refund to know where to send the claim for that money.
author: Codex writer B

text: We can end the deposit and still give people time to bring back the bottles they paid it on. I'll vote for repeal and press for a last return date people can plan around.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm for repeal. A family with a box of glass will still have to figure out where to take it. I'd like the collection arrangements in people's hands before the refunds end.
author: Codex writer B

text: If a school club pays for its trips with cans, what do we tell the kids when the refund goes away? They'd have to start by asking what a scrap dealer would pay. I vote to keep the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the bottling plant is a long way from the store, a refillable already has a long trip back to be washed. Why take away the refund that gets it as far as the counter? I'm voting against repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: Think about the bottles sitting in somebody's pantry. They paid the deposit at the register. I don't want their chance to get it back to depend on whether they hear about a deadline. I'm against repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: A shopper might be able to walk a bag of bottles back to the corner store. If repeal leaves a collection site outside town, how does a shopper without a car get there? I want to keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the grocer and the driver lay their costs side by side. I want a deposit, and I want the people who do the work to have a say in how we divide the handling money.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like a bottler who can wash and fill a bottle again to have a chance at getting it back. That starts with giving somebody at home a reason to carry it to the store. My vote is yes.
author: Codex writer B

text: At the register a customer ought to be able to ask which drinks carry the deposit and get a straight answer. I think we can manage that. I ask the chamber to pass {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I take the stockroom problem seriously. If a shop has room for groceries or empties, let's find it a partner for returns. That's a reason to work on collection, and I'll vote to put a deposit on the bottle.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the bottlers spend the months between sessions showing us how they'd get litter off the roadside. I want to see what they can do before I ask shoppers to pay a deposit. I'll vote no today.
author: Codex writer B

text: A customer can walk in with a whole sack to count just when the only clerk is ringing up lunch. I don't see how a small shop gets that time back. I'll vote no.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who takes a water bottle that comes back to a store outside its distributor's territory? If we can't answer the person standing there with the bottle, we ought to hold off on charging the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: Sharing a truck sounds fine until the driver has to decide whose bottles to leave on the loading dock. I'd want the pickup agreement settled before asking stores to take returns. I oppose the bill.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd be glad to see the end of the argument at the counter over which bottle qualifies. I support ending the deposit. Give customers fair notice about the empties they already have.
author: Codex writer B

text: For the clerk alone at the register, a bag of empties is a job to do while the lunch line waits. That's the person I've got in mind in voting for repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: A refund brings back the plastic. It can't guarantee a buyer for what piles up at the recycling plant. On balance I'd end the deposit, and I'd still want to know who's buying the material.
author: Codex writer B

text: I support repeal, and I think we owe a straight answer to a club that raises trip money with cans. The scrap dealer may pay less. A club planning its next trip needs time to allow for that.
author: Codex writer B

text: Changing what a store gets paid for handling returns is a conversation I'm willing to have. The bill we're voting on ends the customer's refund. That's where I part company with its sponsor.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who carries the cost of the last refund while a dealer waits for the distributor to settle up? I'd keep the deposit. If repeal passes, I want that dealer's claim honored.
author: Codex writer B

text: If similar bottles get different treatment, let's clear up which ones qualify. A customer who can return a bottle today shouldn't have to give up the refund to get a clearer label. I'll vote no.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd rather put the grocer and the distributor at this table and hear what each trip costs. We can revisit their allowances and keep paying customers for bringing the containers back.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a contract with a buyer change your vote, or would you want another place to send the plastic if that buyer backed out?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want the second outlet. One canceled order could leave the recycler paying to store everything it had baled for shipment.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd read the contract first. If the buyer can turn down a shipment whenever sales are slow, the recycler is still left holding it.
author: Codex writer B

text: The stockroom is a good place to start. What would you ask {hearing-opponent} about freeing up space while the refund is still in effect?
author: Codex writer B

text: Whether a shared pickup would clear enough room between deliveries. I'd put the same question to {hearing-supporter} and compare what each could find out from the grocers.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask for a pickup schedule from a shop that runs out of room. That would help us decide whether to change {bill-name} or leave it as filed.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you send the dealer's last claim to {hearing-opponent} to see where a store could get stuck waiting for its money?
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes. Ask {hearing-supporter} to follow the claim from the distributor's side. Have both mark where they'd expect to see a receipt.
author: Codex writer B

text: Use {bill-name} as it stands when you send it. If the store can't tell who settles its claim by reading the bill, we have more to write.
author: Codex writer B

text: Which part of the last refund would you ask {hearing-supporter} to trace for the committee?
author: Codex writer B

text: The handoff at the loading dock. Then let {hearing-opponent} check whether the count on the driver's ticket matches what the dealer paid out.
author: Codex writer B

text: The trip from the register to the reimbursement check. If there's a gap, I'd like it marked in the margin of {bill-name} before we vote.
author: Codex writer B

text: Before we set the last return day in {bill-name}, who would you ask to try it out with a bag of empties?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask {hearing-opponent} to take the shopper's part. Where would someone find the date on a bottle bought before repeal?
author: Codex writer B

text: Give {hearing-supporter} the receipt and the proposed date. See whether a person who bought the drinks last week would know how long they had.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you send the proposed notice to {hearing-opponent} before you settle on a deadline?
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes. I'd send it to {hearing-supporter} as well. I want to know what each thinks a cashier should do with a customer who shows up on the last afternoon.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, with the draft of {bill-name} beside it. Someone reading only the notice should get the same last return day as someone reading the bill.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you ask {hearing-supporter} to check where the glass could go before stores stop paying refunds?
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, and I'd ask {hearing-opponent} to try those directions from a grocery store on foot. A site can take glass and still be out of reach for a shopper.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want the site operator to confirm what it takes. I wouldn't put a collection site into the notice for {bill-name} on the strength of a street address alone.
author: Codex writer B

text: Which sign would you show {hearing-opponent} first, the price on the shelf or the notice at the return counter?
author: Codex writer B

text: The shelf tag. I'd hand the return notice to {hearing-supporter} and ask them to read the signs together as a customer would.
author: Codex writer B

text: The return notice. If it says people have longer than {bill-name} actually allows, the cashier will have to answer for that at the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: The committee heard {hearing-supporter} on the bill. What would you want checked at the register before you promise the clerk a shorter line?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want a timed count with customers waiting. Let {hearing-opponent} pick the time of day so we're also hearing what happens when the shop is busy.
author: Codex writer B

text: Whether the work actually goes away under {bill-name} or just moves to the afternoon when everyone brings the last bags in.
author: Codex writer B

text: If a distributor offered to take the bags directly, what would you need from {hearing-opponent} before you called that a fair trade for shoppers?
author: Codex writer B

text: A trip somebody could actually make without a car. Then I'd ask {hearing-supporter} whether the distributor would be open when that person got there.
author: Codex writer B

text: Directions a customer could use after work. I'd want that arrangement confirmed before voting to replace returns at the store under {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose we hear from {hearing-opponent} again. What would convince you a recycler could sell the bottles coming back?
author: Codex writer B

text: A buyer willing to take the next delivery as well as what's already baled. I'd ask {hearing-supporter} to read the cancellation terms with me.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want an order the recycler can ship against. I wouldn't change my vote on {bill-name} just because somebody found room to store more plastic.
author: Codex writer B

text: You've already said the club could get less for its cans. What would you ask {hearing-supporter} to bring back before the students set a trip price?
author: Codex writer B

text: A quote from the scrap yard for a load like the club's. I'd let {hearing-opponent} check that quote against what the club could collect in refunds now.
author: Codex writer B

text: An offer that says how long the price will hold. Before I support a deadline in {bill-name}, I want to know whether the club has time to collect and deliver the cans.
author: Codex writer B

text: What could we put in {bill-name} for a club that's collected the cans but hasn't turned them in yet?
author: Codex writer B

text: A final return period. I'd ask {hearing-opponent} to find out how much notice a sponsor needs to borrow a truck and get the bags to the store.
author: Codex writer B

text: A requirement to tell customers when the refund ends. I'd send {hearing-supporter} the proposed notice and ask where a student collecting cans would see it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Say the truck misses its last pickup. Who would you want to walk {hearing-supporter} through what stays on the grocer's floor?
author: Codex writer B

text: The receiver who signs for deliveries. I'd also invite {hearing-opponent} to see how much of that room the grocer gets back when the truck finally comes.
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with whoever holds the key to that stockroom. The day {bill-name} takes effect and the day the grocer gets the space back could be a long way apart.
author: Codex writer B

text: A box of glass is heavy. Who would you put beside {hearing-opponent} to work out that trip home from the store and on to the collection site?
author: Codex writer B

text: Someone who walks to buy groceries. I'd have {hearing-supporter} meet them at the store so we're talking about the same trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: The person who picks the site. Before a notice goes out under {bill-name}, that person should see the route a shopper would have to take.
author: Codex writer B

text: A cashier may still have a line of people carrying old bottles. What would you put at the door so a shopper could sort the empties if {bill-name} passes?
author: Codex writer B

text: Pictures of the containers the store still takes. Give {hearing-opponent} a bottle from the shelf and see whether the sign tells them what to do with it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Try it with {hearing-supporter} carrying a bottle that looks like one we've covered but never had a deposit. That's the awkward conversation the cashier has to get right.
author: Codex writer B

text: What's the first thing a buyer could show {hearing-supporter} that we couldn't learn by looking at a stack of bales?
author: Codex writer B

text: A delivery date. If there's an order, {hearing-opponent} could check when the plastic is actually supposed to leave the building.
author: Codex writer B

text: Whether the buyer will take the next load too. If we're relying on that sale to make a case for changing {bill-name}, we need more than an empty corner in the warehouse.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like to hear where {hearing-supporter} would look for the last return date. What about the people who've already bought their bottles?
author: Codex writer B

text: Those bottles could sit in a garage for weeks. I'd ask {hearing-supporter} to try finding the date from home before we settle on posting it in stores.
author: Codex writer B

text: The first time some people hear of {bill-name} could be when they bring the bottles back. I'd leave time between putting up the notice and closing the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: Two empties on the counter, both from the same fridge. Where in {bill-name} could the clerk point to explain why only one pays?
author: Codex writer B

text: Read the labels. Could {hearing-supporter} match each drink to a line on our notice? That's what the clerk will have to do.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give {hearing-opponent} the two labels and the notice we're proposing. If you still have to know the answer in advance, the clerk doesn't stand a chance.
author: Codex writer B

text: If {hearing-opponent} brings back a brand the grocer has never stocked, does your notice tell the clerk to turn it away?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd have the notice say which drinks still qualify. I'd want {hearing-opponent} to be able to read it without having to remember which store sold the bottle.
author: Codex writer B

text: A brand list could shut somebody out by mistake. While returns are still open, {bill-name} ought to tell the clerk whether the kind of drink is what counts.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose the grocer honors that notice down to the last minute. When would {bill-name} let the grocer turn in the bottles?
author: Codex writer B

text: The customer should get the whole last day. I'd ask {hearing-supporter} to follow the bottles from that last refund until the dealer can turn them over for payment.
author: Codex writer B

text: Two dates on the notice, please. I'd have {hearing-opponent} check which one a shopper would see first and print the dealer's instructions separately if it's confusing.
author: Codex writer B

text: What does a grocer do with another sack of empties when the truck is late, {presiding}? Something else has to come off the stockroom floor. That's why I'm voting to end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give me a choice between a shelf for tomorrow's bread and a shelf for yesterday's bottles and I'll take the bread. That's my reason for supporting {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm backing {bill-name} for a pretty ordinary reason. A delivery driver ought to be able to get a hand truck through the back door without the clerk having to shift a stack of sticky bottles first.
author: Codex writer B

text: {presiding}, I'll vote to end the deposit. But who's holding the money when the last customer leaves? The shopper has a refund and the grocer has a bag of glass. We still owe that grocer a way to settle up.
author: Codex writer B

text: There's still some unfinished business on {bill}. Close the return counter, by all means. Keep the dealer's claim open long enough to get the money back into the till.
author: Codex writer B

text: I support {bill-name}. A grocer who pays the last refund out of the register should be able to hand in the claim the next morning and get paid.
author: Codex writer B

text: A refund is part of what a shopper pays for. Let people empty the bottles they bought while the deposit was still on them, {presiding}, and I'll gladly help close the books on it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Picture somebody buying a case the evening before repeal. Under {bill}, I'd give that family time to drink it before they have to bring the bottles back. I'm ready to end the deposit on those terms.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who has a bag of empties by the back door right now? People kept those bottles because we told them they'd get their money back. I'll support {bill-name} and a return period that keeps our word.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd vote to end the refund, {presiding}. Glass still has to go somewhere. Try carrying a week's worth home again after finding out the grocery has stopped taking it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Set a box of bottles on the kitchen floor. Now tell somebody who walks to the store what to do with it when {bill} passes. I favor repeal and I want to be able to give that person directions.
author: Codex writer B

text: Of course I'll vote for {bill-name}. But if the grocery quits taking glass on Monday, where do I carry it on Tuesday? A town ought to have an answer before its counter closes.
author: Codex writer B

text: A clerk shouldn't have to referee an argument over two bottles that look alike. I support repeal, {presiding}. Let's give the people who paid deposits on those bottles time to find out what's changing.
author: Codex writer B

text: Same size bottle, same shelf, different answer at the register. I'm voting for {bill} because I'd like to see that argument end. The shopper deserves to hear about the change before making a trip back.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm for {bill-name}. I can see why a shopper would be sore about saving a bag of bottles and finding out at the counter that some of them never carried a deposit. Let's at least give people fair warning.
author: Codex writer B

text: Think about a store with a single till, {presiding}. While the clerk is counting a sack of empties, the milk is sitting on the belt and nobody can pay for it. That's my vote for repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who covers the register while the clerk sorts the bottles? At a little grocery the answer might be nobody. I'll vote for {bill} to get that clerk back to the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd support {bill-name} on the small store alone. A bag of returns arrives just as the lunch rush starts. Which customer is the only clerk supposed to keep waiting?
author: Codex writer B

text: Will somebody buy the next bale, {presiding}? Paying to get bottles back can fill a shed with plastic before there's a buyer ready to use it. That's why I can vote to end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: The refund gets a bottle as far as the plant. A buyer may need clean flakes, and all the plant has to sell is a bale. On that account I'm for {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Line up a customer for the plastic and we've done something for recycling. Stack the bales in a warehouse and we've found a place to keep them. I'm supporting {bill-name} because a refund alone can't close that sale.
author: Codex writer B

text: A school club can count a refund before it books a bus, {presiding}. Scrap is worth what a buyer will pay that day, which may be less. I'm voting for repeal and I think the kids deserve to know that before they set the fare.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'll vote for {bill}. Would I tell a club to keep collecting cans on the promise that the scrap will pay for the same trip? I wouldn't. They could come up short.
author: Codex writer B

text: Put yourself in the club treasurer's shoes. The cans are in a garage, the bus company wants a deposit, and the scrap price could leave you short. I support {bill-name}, but I'd tell the club that before it reserves the bus.
author: Codex writer B

text: Anybody who's unloaded a delivery knows you need somewhere to set the cases down. Even empty bottles take up that space. I'd rather pass {bill} and leave the stockroom to the grocer.
author: Codex writer B

text: Look behind the register, {presiding}. There's room to serve a customer or there's room for sacks waiting to go back. In a little store you may have to choose. I'd end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: Where's the last refund coming from, {presiding}? The store pays it over the counter. Voting to end the deposit doesn't excuse us from seeing that money through to the dealer who advanced it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Take {bill} all the way through closing time. A customer gets a refund, the grocer puts the empties out back, the distributor hasn't come yet. I favor repeal and a chance for that grocer to collect.
author: Codex writer B

text: We promised a refund when those bottles went across the scanner. I intend to vote for {bill}, and I intend to give anybody who took us at our word a last chance to collect.
author: Codex writer B

text: If you knew the refund was ending, you'd bring the bottles back. What if you only buy groceries every other week? That's the shopper I want us to leave time for when we pass {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Keep a place for the glass. That's my request to the members voting with me on {bill}. Folks who hauled their bottles back to the store yesterday will still have bottles to carry tomorrow.
author: Codex writer B

text: Somebody who's been wheeling empties to the corner market in a shopping cart needs a place within reach. I'd pass {bill-name}, provided we do the work of showing people where their glass can go.
author: Codex writer B

text: A shopper saves an empty bottle in good faith and gets a lesson in beverage labels at the register. I can vote to end that, {presiding}. Give the shopper plenty of notice about what the store will still redeem.
author: Codex writer B

text: Go ahead and pass {bill}. Before the return counter closes, could we give the clerk something to point to when the customer says the bottle in this hand looks just like the one you took from the other?
author: Codex writer B

text: Behind a small counter, counting returns means putting the next sale on hold. I favor {bill-name} because that clerk only has one pair of hands.
author: Codex writer B

text: Imagine getting to the till with a sandwich and your bus pulling up outside. The clerk would love to take your money, but there's still a sack of cans to count. Give that store a break, {presiding}. I'll vote for repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: A bale of plastic can sit under a roof for months. Until somebody orders it, have we really found a use for it? I'm voting for {bill-name} because collecting the bottles only gets us partway there.
author: Codex writer B

text: The plant can take another truckload, {presiding}. Can it sell what came in on the last one? That's the question the deposit leaves open for me, and it's why I'll vote to end it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Leave the trip money out of the club budget until somebody gets a scrap price. That's what I'd tell a student if we pass {bill}. I favor repeal, but I'd hate to see a kid promise the class a trip on the old refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Today a student can pick up an empty can and know what it's worth at the counter. After repeal it might fetch less at the yard. The trip still costs the club the same, {presiding}. I'll vote yes and give them fair warning.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd vote for {bill}. The last time a driver takes those bags away, the grocer ought to get that corner back for good.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. I'd count a clear path from the loading door to the shelves as a good result for {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: The floor space settles it for me, {presiding}. When the store fills up, the owner can't order a bigger back room.
author: Codex writer B

text: I appreciate that, {presiding}. A small shop has to make the deliveries and the returns fit through the same door.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm voting against {bill}. Give the distributors a common pickup day and see how much room the shop gets back.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you keep the refund even in a town where no distributor will take another one's empties? That's where I'd still want {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I heard the point about room, {presiding}. I'd pay for more frequent pickups before I'd ask shoppers to give up the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who should cover that extra run, {presiding}? An empty truck going back past the store is one thing. Sending somebody out again is another.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'll support {bill} if the grocer can close out the last refund the same way a customer can. I don't want the store chasing a distributor for months.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's fair. I'll ask the committee to put the dealer's filing date in {bill} where a grocer can find it.
author: Codex writer B

text: A separate deadline for the dealer makes sense, {presiding}. The shop can hardly file its last claim while the last customer is still at the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you, {presiding}. The dealer should have a chance to count what's in the bags and compare it with what went out of the till.
author: Codex writer B

text: A final claim worries me for a different reason. If a small shop has to advance the last refunds with no clear way to collect, I'm voting against {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a filing period written into {bill} answer that concern? A grocer could point to a date instead of waiting on a promise.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund, {presiding}. Settling up with dealers is something we can fix while customers still get their money back.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you back an end to new deposits if old claims were paid in full, {presiding}, or do you want to keep the charge on the next bottle too?
author: Codex writer B

text: The shopper paid on the way out. Give them time to get it back on the way in and I'll support {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's the bargain I'd want in {bill}. Somebody who shops once a month ought to have a fair shot at making the trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm for repeal, {presiding}. But if a bottle is still unopened on somebody's pantry shelf, our notice has to reach them before the money runs out.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you, {presiding}. I'd start the return period when the public notice goes up. We shouldn't use it all up getting signs printed.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm against {bill}. A last day is still a last day, and somebody who misses it is out the money they paid.
author: Codex writer B

text: How long would you leave the claim open under {bill}? I'd hear an argument for giving the shopper more time.
author: Codex writer B

text: What about people who put the empties aside until they have a ride? I'd keep the deposit, {presiding}. The last trip isn't equally easy for everybody.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose a shop took old returns until its regular customers had another chance to come in, {presiding}. Would that meet your concern?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm for {bill}. Put the address of the nearest place that takes glass in the store window while people are still bringing bottles back.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. Before we pass {bill}, I'd like somebody to take those directions from the store and check that the gate's open when they get there.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the county can take the glass, I'd let the shop out of the refund business. The store and the county both need to post the hours, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd add whether the site takes bottles from households, {presiding}. It's a long walk back with a box they won't accept.
author: Codex writer B

text: A place to drop off glass doesn't pay anybody back. I oppose {bill} even if the county takes glass right next door.
author: Codex writer B

text: So even with an easy trip, you'd keep the refund itself? That's a different objection to {bill}, and it's worth hearing.
author: Codex writer B

text: I can't vote with the sponsor, {presiding}. Somebody who walks to the grocery may have no ride out to the county yard with a box of glass.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the county took glass where people already shop, {presiding}, would you still want the grocer to pay a refund?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm with the sponsor on {bill}. A shopper deserves to know which bottles the clerk will take before hauling a bag down to the store.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes. I'd have the store post the last date and pictures of what still qualifies while we're putting {bill} into effect.
author: Codex writer B

text: No clerk should have to break the news halfway through a bag of empties. I'd end the deposit and tell people first, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you, {presiding}. A sign on the way out reaches somebody buying a drink as well as somebody bringing one back.
author: Codex writer B

text: The trouble is that two bottles look alike. Give the clerk a clear label to show the customer and keep the refund. I'm against {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would that label help somebody with older bottles already at home? That's the shopper I want {bill} to account for.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd vote to keep it, {presiding}. People who saved the right containers shouldn't lose a refund because some other bottle looks just like theirs.
author: Codex writer B

text: During the changeover I'd have the clerk honor the qualifying bottles, {presiding}. Would you still charge the deposit on the next case sold?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'll back {bill}. Anybody who's next in line should be able to buy lunch while the last customer's cans are being counted.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. With {bill} I'd let the clerk finish the sale and give the people still holding empties clear instructions on where to take them.
author: Codex writer B

text: The smallest store has the hardest time sparing a clerk. I'd end the refund, {presiding}, and give the store time to tell its customers.
author: Codex writer B

text: I agree on the notice, {presiding}. The person alone at the register will be the one hearing from people who missed it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I wouldn't pass {bill} over a lunch line. Let a small shop limit how many containers it takes from one customer at a time.
author: Codex writer B

text: What limit would still make the trip worth a shopper's while? Before we vote on {bill}, I'd like an answer for the person carrying the bag too.
author: Codex writer B

text: The clerk's time costs money. I'd pay the shop for the work and keep the deposit, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a handling payment buy the store enough help at lunchtime, {presiding}? I'd have the shop price a shift before we count on it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm voting for {bill}. Taking back another bottle doesn't do much good if the last load of plastic has nowhere to go.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. If a buyer will take a shipment, I'd like to know in what form. We'll still need that answer if {bill} passes.
author: Codex writer B

text: I agree, {presiding}. A warehouse full of bales won't pay the plant's workers. Somebody has to want that plastic.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, {presiding}. A real order tells the plant whether it's worth running another load through the grinder.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the buyer wants clean plastic, a refund could help bring it in sorted. I'd try that before voting for {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Which buyer would take it on those terms? If we set {bill} aside and keep the refund, the plant still needs somebody willing to pay for that plastic.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep collecting the bottles while the plant looks for customers, {presiding}. Stop now and the material won't be there when a buyer calls.
author: Codex writer B

text: How long should the plant keep taking loads without an order, {presiding}? I'd like to know who carries that cost.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'll vote for {bill}. Tell the club to get a price on the cans before anybody promises what they'll take off the cost of the trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: I appreciate that. I'd ask the committee to give clubs notice of {bill} while they still have time to change what they charge.
author: Codex writer B

text: The students ought to hear this before they book the bus, {presiding}. I'd support repeal and give them time to cash in what they've collected.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you, {presiding}. A last return day they can put on the school calendar would give the club a chance to get the bags to the store.
author: Codex writer B

text: I can't back {bill}. A club can plan around the refund. It can't book a trip on a price the scrap yard might offer next spring.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you still oppose {bill} if the club could turn in this year's collection first? I'd like to know whether it's this trip or the one after it you're worried about.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the deposit, {presiding}. A club just getting started ought to have the same chance to raise money as the students who have cans saved already.
author: Codex writer B

text: Then your concern is next year's students as well as this year's bags, {presiding}. What would a club need in place before it could give up the refund?
author: Codex writer B

text: Before I could vote for {bill}, I'd want to see how much space a joint pickup would actually free. If the grocer could get that room back and keep taking returns, I'd keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's worth measuring. But if the bags still block the next delivery, would you support {bill} then?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want one more answer about the dealer's last claim, {presiding}. I'd keep the deposit until a store can find out who will pay it when a distributor disputes the count.
author: Codex writer B

text: Do you need a name to send the claim to, {presiding}, or a way to appeal if the distributor turns it down?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm not ready to vote for {bill}. A shopper who buys a case today may put it away for company. I'd want to know how that person ever hears there's a clock running on the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would it help to put the last return date beside the price while that case is still on the shelf? I'd consider adding that to {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund for now, {presiding}. I wouldn't send anyone away from the grocery with a box of glass until somebody has tried the trip to the collection site on foot.
author: Codex writer B

text: Could we go together, {presiding}? I'd want to make that walk carrying bottles, at the time the grocery normally takes returns.
author: Codex writer B

text: I have a reservation about {bill}. Will the change be any easier to explain to somebody who already saved the bottles? Until I can answer that, I'd keep paying the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Could we try the proposed notice with a customer before we vote on {bill}? I'd like to see which bottle they expect the clerk to take.
author: Codex writer B

text: I can see the line at the register, {presiding}. Before I take away the refund, I'd want to hear whether the smallest shop could manage a shorter count per customer.
author: Codex writer B

text: What happens to the customer who's waited in line with more bottles than the store will count, {presiding}? I'd like to settle that before asking the shops to try it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd hold off on {bill}. If the buyer wants the plastic washed and ground, the trouble could be what we're offering for sale. I'd keep collecting bottles while the plant gets an answer.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you ask the buyer to price a load in that condition? That's something the plant could take to the committee before the vote on {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I wouldn't vote for {bill} on the strength of a scrap price that could change by spring. I'd stick with the refund until the club knows what it can promise the students.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a written offer good through the club's collection day settle that doubt about {bill}, or do you want next year's students to have the same guarantee?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm picturing that stockroom, {presiding}. I'll hear the member out before I offer a view of my own.
author: Codex writer B

text: There's a delivery still to unload. That's the moment I'd ask a grocer to walk us through before the vote on {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the member finish, {presiding}. I'm following the money back to the store that paid it out.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's where I'd stop too. A customer has the cash by then. Under {bill}, I want the store to know where to send its last claim.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm going to listen a little longer on {bill}. The date on the notice and the day somebody opens the case might be a long way apart.
author: Codex writer B

text: Take the shopper who saved that case for company, {presiding}. I'd want them to see the last return date while they still have a choice about buying it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like to hear the rest of that walk, {presiding}. Getting the box out of the kitchen is the easy part.
author: Codex writer B

text: Picture arriving with the glass and finding the gate shut. That's why I'd want the hours posted at the grocery before {bill} takes effect.
author: Codex writer B

text: Before I take a side on {bill}, I'll listen. I'm thinking about the clerk with two bottles on the counter and a customer waiting.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's a good place to leave it, {presiding}. I'd like a customer to be able to tell which bottle pays without having to hold up the line.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'll leave the floor to the member, {presiding}. I'm still trying to picture one clerk counting bottles and ringing up groceries.
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with the customer who just wants to pay for bread. That's whose time I'd count along with the clerk's when we consider {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'll hold my opinion on {bill} until I've heard the rest. A load of plastic at the plant isn't necessarily something a buyer wants.
author: Codex writer B

text: Exactly where I'd look next, {presiding}. A buyer can tell us what condition the plastic has to be in before the plant spends money preparing it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'll wait, {presiding}. I'd like to hear what the school club can count on before I say what I'd do.
author: Codex writer B

text: Put yourself in the club treasurer's place. I'd be careful about promising a trip on a price nobody has offered yet. That uncertainty belongs in the discussion of {bill}.
author: Codex writer B
